newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UNICEF accuses baby milk makers of breaching code.
newsitem.headline: UNICEF accuses baby milk makers of breaching code.

text.p: The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) on Tuesday accused multinational baby-food companies of putting infant lives at risk by aggressively promoting breast-milk substitutes.
The agency called on companies to disclose their marketing practices in each country and prove their compliance with a voluntary code adopted by the U.N.'s World Health Organisation (WHO).

UNICEF backed a study released last week in London by an international group monitoring breast-feeding world-wide which found the code was being violated in Bangladesh, Poland, Thailand and South Africa.

The report, entitled "Cracking the Code", was issued by a coalition of 27 churches, academic bodies, infant feeding experts and development groups. It named Gerber, a subsidiary of Switzerland's Sandoz AG, Mead Johnson, Nestle AG, Nutricia and Wyeth as being among those violating the code in four states.
Last year, Sandoz merged with another Swiss pharmaceutical firm, Ciba-Geigy, to form Novartis.
The WHO argues that while mothers' milk is hygienic and passes on antibodies that enable babies to fight disease, substitutes involve adding water which is often contaminated in the developing world.
UNICEF, in a statement issued in Geneva, endorsed the coalition's study as a "careful and sound analysis".

"Thus, 16 years after the international code was embraced by the world community, its provisions are still being breached on a continuing basis," it said. "This puts the health and lives of great numbers of infants at risk."
"Marketing practices that undermine breastfeeding are potentially hazardous wherever they are pursued."
UNICEF appealed to manufacturers and distributors to uphold the provisions of the code, which itself calls on companies to monitor their own marketing practices and ensure they conform.

It urged companies to "set out, country by country, their range of marketing practices, in order to demonstrate, through full disclosure, precisely how those practices are consistent with the international code".
Hind Khatib, coordinator of UNICEF's so-called baby-friendly hospital initiative, was asked which multinational firms violated the code. "All of them," she told a news briefing.
"We are not saying "no' altogether for industry. We are saying give the mother a chance to make an informed decision.
"The code specifically speaks about labelling and marketing techniques and asks for the protection of the mother's decision.
"When industry goes in and starts with their marketing techniques...they are already misleading the mother by giving her a substitute before she even thinks about her breastmilk.

UNICEF spokeswoman Marie Heuze said: "We say that women who decide not to breastfeed their baby must know that their babies may be at risk, in particular if conditions are not adequate, and that the children don't receive their anti-bodies.

"In the developing world they are not given the choice most of the time. We must fight against the free distribution of sample products and the extremely aggressive, subliminal or sophisticated commercial practices which lead women to imagine their social status will improve if they don't breastfeed."
Jim Akre, a technical expert in WHO's food and nutrition division, told Reuters: "We estimate 1.5 million deaths could be averted annually through effective breast-feeding.
"But it can't be known what percent of that figure is attributable to formula feeding," he added.
Breastfeeding rates vary greatly even within continents, according to Akre. More than 95 per cent of Scandinavian women breastfeed, while fewer than one in two French ever do, he said.
"We recommend exclusive breastfeeding for the first four to six months of life," Akre said. "But it really is a cultural question. Attitudes are very different."
